text.p: Wall Street's run up to 6,000 failed to cheer commodity markets from where booming equities and bonds have siphoned speculative money, with the exception of crude oil which powered on with a rally to top $24 per barrel.

Industrial metals were not helped when scrap dealer Herbert Black of Canada whose selling of the market earlier this year helped topple Japan's trading idol, Yasuo Hamanaka, took a "bearish" view of the copper price.

He predicted at an industry convention that London Metal Exchange (LME) three-months copper might slip to $1,400 per tonne in 1998 under a weight of new production and of metal previously hoarded by Japan's Sumitomo Corp and others. Hamanaka had held big stocks of copper before his June 14 dismissal by Sumitomo Corp and its accusations that he ran up losses of $2.6 billion on maverick trades.
Black was among dealers who sensed that his long position was vulnerable and who sold against him.
Copper ended London's afternoon just above $1,900 per tonne and easier from Friday on a day when sluggish range trading characterized most commodities except oil.
Aluminium dropped to its lowest in nearly 2-1/2 years at $1,332 a tonne, the weakest since May 1994. Brokers cited high stocks and a weak technical chart outlook.
But world benchmark November futures for North Sea crude oil broke back above $24 and stood 30 cents up on the day at $24.15 per barrel before easing slightly.
A scramble to recharge depleted winter heating oil stocks in Europe and the United States kept prices on the boil.
Worried refinery buyers, concerned that an early US cold snap could erode depleted stocks, hedged against price rises on futures exchanges and speculators bet on further gains.

All three legs of the NYMEX oil complex hit contract highs Monday with gasoline posting the sharpest gains after a recent string of maintenance-related output cuts was capped off by problems at a large BP America refinery.
November crude was buoyed by the rally in refined product prices, ending 51 cents higher at $25.24 a barrel after rising to a contract high of $25.28.

Gold stabilised after a fall below $380 per ounce early last week and traded little changed to close in London at $380.15. It edged up later. In New York, spot gold ended quoted $380.35/380.85 an ounce, compared to the London Monday afternoon fix at $380.10, and Friday's New York close around $380.25.

CBOT wheat futures closed mixed with nearby months firm on a rally in corn and soybean futures with news India has halted wheat exports also viewed as supportive, traders said. Deferred months ended lower on bull spreading with good wheat seeding weather in U.S. winter wheat growing regions also weighing on the new crop July, they said. Bombay traders Friday said Indian wheat exports had ground to a halt as a state agency had not issued export licenses due to a shortage of government-owned supplies. Many market watchers said trading in wheat was very quiet and gave a nod to corn and soybeans as Monday's floor leader. Wheat closed 1-1/2 cents per bushel higher to three cents lower, with December up 1-1/2 at $4.22-1/2.

CSCE world sugar futures settled a thinly-traded session weaker, with activity stymied by a dearth of physical news, a balanced technical picture and a golf outing which took several players out of the ring, market sources said.
Volume was estimated at a mere 6,095 lots.

While March climbed to resistance seen in the mid-10.90 cent a lb range, the contract was unable to hold gains and fell to its low. Prices did not stray from their current trading range, however, with support seen at 10.75 and then at 10.60.
The March contract eased 0.05 on the day to close at 10.88, having ranged from 10.94 to 10.83. The back months settled 0.04 lower to 0.01 firmer.
